doc.title: Bob Havens interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: War years, family circumstances and segregated minstrel shows
summary: His father's background and modest income, and playing in minstrel shows for servicemen; the local audience was segregated.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: How did World War II affect your community, your family, or just your daily life?

Well of course I was in school and my father did not have much formal schooling, I think he had to quit when he was about eight years old and go to work. He came from a community in Indiana, Kokomo, and he had to go to work in the foundry there. And then he sort of migrated from Indiana to Illinois, after a divorce in his family, then he moved on and he and my mother I think were married about 1921. And I didn’t come along until 1930. So my father, due to his lack of education, he was kind of like a custodian in a school. And we were not considered much more than somewhere in between a poor and medium income family. And so I didn’t have the real finer things of life. But I did have my records and my sheet music and as far as I was concerned I had everything I wanted. But I did grow up in the war years there. And as a matter of fact I became involved in a lot of community music activities at that age. And I played, entertained the servicemen in World War II. We had — in those days we had minstrel shows you know. And I think it’s sort of outlawed these days, we don’t do that anymore. But I was involved in some local minstrel shows and we traveled around to various Army camps and put on shows for them. And I played in the pit orchestra along with my father and he also was a very strong bass singer, besides playing the bass fiddle.
Were these minstrel shows, when you did it for the servicemen, were the audiences segregated so that you were playing just for the white soldiers?

Yes. That’s the way I remember it. Well I don’t remember what happened in the Army camps. But when we played locally in Quincy it was a segregated audience at that time. I wasn’t aware of any segregation at that time. It just didn’t register with me that that’s what was going on you know. But it was fun. I enjoyed playing the shows. We had the “end men” in blackface. My father was a member of the chorus I guess you’d call it. And he would have a bass solo and sang a number in the program. But I played in the pit orchestra. But that was one activity that I had during the war years. Then I was a member of the drum and bugle corps. I started out in that when I was twelve years old and I played the baritone bugle. And that was a lot of fun. And we were sponsored by the American Legion Club in Quincy and we entered contests, the corps contests in the State of Illinois, and that continued from when I was about twelve years old through about age eighteen I guess, all the way through my high school days.
